1.o: Here we first meet with Nehemiah at the Persian court, where we find him, I. Inquisitive concerning the state of the Jews and Jerusalem, ver. 1, 2. II. Informed of their deplorable condition, ver. 3. III. Fasting and praying thereupon (ver. 4), with a particular account of his prayer, ver. 5-11. Such is the rise of this great man, by piety, not by policy.
1.i: Nehemiah hears that Jerusalem's walls are in ruins, prays for four months, and then asks the Persian king to let him go and rebuild.
1.p: Lord, You care about the broken places. Give us hearts that hurt for what hurts You. Amen.
1.l: Say a quick prayer, even just a few words, before you do something hard today.
q: Nehemiah prayed for months and then prayed in a moment. When do you pray?

2.o: How Nehemiah wrestled with God and prevailed we read in the foregoing chapter; now here we are told how, like Jacob, he prevailed with men also, and so found that his prayers were heard and answered. I. He prevailed with the king to send him to Jerusalem with a commission to build a wall about it, and grant him what was necessary for it, ver. 1-8. II. He prevailed against the enemies that would have obstructed him in his journey (ver. 9-11) and laughed him out of his undertaking, ver. 19, 20. III.
2.i: Nehemiah hears that Jerusalem's walls are in ruins, prays for four months, and then asks the Persian king to let him go and rebuild.
2.p: Lord, You care about the broken places. Give us hearts that hurt for what hurts You. Amen.
2.l: Say a quick prayer, even just a few words, before you do something hard today.
q: Nehemiah prayed for months and then prayed in a moment. When do you pray?

3.o: Saying and doing are often two things: many are ready to say, "Let us rise up and build," who sit still and do nothing, like that fair-spoken son who said,"I go, Sir, but went not." The undertakers here were none of those. As soon as they had resolved to build the wall about Jerusalem they lost no time, but set about it presently, as we find in this chapter. Let it never be said that we left that good work to be done to-morrow which we might as well have done to-day. This chapter gives an account of two things:—I.
3.s: Everyone Builds Opposite Their Own House
3.i: Nehemiah 3 is a list of names and sections that shows how a whole city rebuilt its wall together.
3.p: Lord, You build with many hands. Show us our section of the wall, and keep us from leaving the work to others. Amen.
3.l: Do the job in front of you today, the small one nearest to you, and do it well.
q: The leader's own share is not mentioned. Whose share in your work are you most quietly relying on?

4.o: We left all hands at work for the building of the wall about Jerusalem. But such good work is not wont to be carried on without opposition; now here we are told what opposition was given to it, and what methods Nehemiah took to forward the work, notwithstanding that opposition. I. Their enemies reproached and ridiculed their undertaking, but their scoffs they answered with prayers: they heeded them not, but went on with their work notwithstanding, ver. 1-6. II.
4.s: A Trowel in One Hand, a Weapon in the Other
4.i: Enemies mock and threaten the builders, so Nehemiah has half the men work and half guard the wall.
4.p: Lord, You fight for us. Keep us working at what You have given us, and keep us watchful. Amen.
4.l: When something you are doing is hard, pray, and then keep working.
q: Nehemiah prayed and posted a guard. When do you need to do both?

5.o: How bravely Nehemiah, as a wise and faithful governor, stood upon his guard against the attacks of enemies abroad, we read in the foregoing chapter. Here we have him no less bold and active to redress grievances at home, and, having kept them from being destroyed by their enemies, to keep them from destroying one another. Here is, I. The complaint which the poor made to him of the great hardships which the rich (of whom they were forced to borrow money) put upon them, ver. 1-5. II.
5.i: Nehemiah 5 interrupts the wall-building with a crisis inside the city: people were crushing their own neighbors with debt.
5.p: Lord, You care for the poor and the borrower. Make us fair and generous, and keep us from profiting from another person's need. Amen.
5.l: Share something with someone who has less than you today, without expecting anything back.
q: Hard-heartedness among believers exposes religion to reproach. Who is hurt by how you handle money?

6.o: The cries of oppressed poverty being stilled, we are now to enquire how the building of the wall goes forward, and in this chapter we find it carried on with vigour and finished with joy, notwithstanding the restless attempts of the gates of hell to hinder it. How the Jews' enemies were baffled in their design to put a stop to it by force we read before, ch. iv. Here we find how their endeavours to drive Nehemiah off from it were frustrated. I.
6.i: The wall of Jerusalem is finished in fifty-two days and dedicated with two choirs on its top.
6.p: Lord, You rebuild what is broken. We give You thanks and praise with all our hearts. Amen.
6.l: Celebrate something good today with your family or friends, and thank God out loud.
q: The joy was heard from far away. What would make your joy loud enough to be heard?

7.o: The success of one good design for God and our generation should encourage us to proceed and form some other; Nehemiah did so, having fortified Jerusalem with gates and walls, his next care is, I. To see the city well kept, ver. 1-4. II. To see it well peopled, in order to which he here reviews and calls over the register of the children of the captivity, the families that returned at first, and records it, ver. 5-73. It is the same, in effect, with that which we had, Ezra ii.
7.s: One in Ten Moves to Jerusalem
7.i: Nehemiah 7 and 11 fill an empty city with people, first by counting, then by lot, and then by volunteers.
7.p: Lord, You make a city by gathering people. Bless every volunteer and every family that makes a place home. Amen.
7.l: Welcome a new person to your neighborhood, school, or church today, and help them feel at home.
q: Heavy work was passed to the people of another race in the temple. Who is carrying a load in your community that others quietly benefit from?

8.o: Ezra came up out of Babylon thirteen years before Nehemiah came, yet we have here a piece of good work which he did, that might have been done before, but was not done till Nehemiah came, who, though he was not such a scholar nor such a divine as Ezra, nor such a scribe in the law of his God, yet was a man of a more lively active spirit. His zeal set Ezra's learning on work, and then great things were done, as we find here, where we have, I. The public and solemn reading and expounding of the law, ver. 1-8. II.
8.s: The Joy of the Lord Is Your Strength
8.i: Ezra reads the Law to the whole people at the Water Gate, the Levites explain it, and the people go from tears to joy.
8.p: Lord, open our ears to hear Your Word, and fill us with Your joy. Amen.
8.l: Read a Bible verse aloud today with someone, and talk about what it means.
q: The people understood the Word and then rejoiced. How do you make sense of the Bible when you read it?

9.o: The tenth day of the seventh month between the feast of trumpets (ch. viii. 2) and the feast of tabernacles (ver. 14) was appointed to be the day of atonement; we have no reason to think but that it was religiously observed, though it is not mentioned. But here we have an account of an occasional fast that was kept a fortnight after that, with reference to the present posture of their affairs, and it was, as that, a day of humiliation. There is a time to weep as well as a time to laugh. We have here an account. I.
9.s: A Day of Confession and a Binding Promise
9.i: Nehemiah 9 and 10 record the longest prayer in the Bible, a retelling of Israel's story, and the signed promise that followed.
9.p: Lord, You are gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in love. Help us keep our promises to You. Amen.
9.l: Say a short prayer today that tells part of God's story and ends with a promise you can keep.
q: What friendship or habit is a snare you have not yet cut?

10.o: We have in this chapter a particular account of the covenant which in the close of the foregoing chapter was resolved upon; they struck while the iron was hot, and immediately put that good resolve in execution, when they were in a good frame, lest, if it should be delayed, it might be dropped. Here we have, I. The names of those that set their hands and seals to it, ver. 1-27. II. An account of those who signified their consent and concurrence, ver. 28, 29. III.
10.s: A Day of Confession and a Binding Promise
10.i: Nehemiah 9 and 10 record the longest prayer in the Bible, a retelling of Israel's story, and the signed promise that followed.
10.p: Lord, You are gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in love. Help us keep our promises to You. Amen.
10.l: Say a short prayer today that tells part of God's story and ends with a promise you can keep.
q: What friendship or habit is a snare you have not yet cut?

11.o: Jerusalem was walled round, but it was not as yet fully inhabited, and therefore was weak and despicable. Nehemiah's next care is to bring people into it; of that we have here an account. I. The methods taken to replenish it, ver. 1, 2. II. The principal persons that resided there, of Judah and Benjamin (ver. 3-9), of the priests and Levites, ver. 10-19. III. The several cities and villages of Judah and Benjamin that were peopled by the rest of their families, ver. 20-36.
11.s: One in Ten Moves to Jerusalem
11.i: Nehemiah 7 and 11 fill an empty city with people, first by counting, then by lot, and then by volunteers.
11.p: Lord, You make a city by gathering people. Bless every volunteer and every family that makes a place home. Amen.
11.l: Welcome a new person to your neighborhood, school, or church today, and help them feel at home.
q: Heavy work was passed to the people of another race in the temple. Who is carrying a load in your community that others quietly benefit from?

12.o: In this chapter are preserved upon record, I. The names of the chief of the priests and the Levites that came up with Zerubbabel, ver. 1-9. II. The succession of the high priests, ver. 10, 11. III. The names of the next generation of the other chief priests, ver. 12-21. IV. The eminent Levites that were in Nehemiah's time, ver. 22-26. V. The solemnity of dedicating the wall of Jerusalem, ver. 27-43. VI. The settling of the offices of the priests and Levites in the temple, ver. 44-47.
12.i: The wall of Jerusalem is finished in fifty-two days and dedicated with two choirs on its top.
12.p: Lord, You rebuild what is broken. We give You thanks and praise with all our hearts. Amen.
12.l: Celebrate something good today with your family or friends, and thank God out loud.
q: The joy was heard from far away. What would make your joy loud enough to be heard?

13.o: Nehemiah, having finished what he undertook for the fencing and filling of the holy city, returned to the king his master, who was not willing to be long without him, as appears (v. 6). But, after some time, he obtained leave to come back again to Jerusalem, to redress grievances, and purge out some corruptions which had crept in in his absence; and very active he was in reforming several abuses, which here we have an account of. I.
13.i: Nehemiah 13 is a sobering last chapter in which, after the great covenant, the problems return.
13.p: Remember us, O God, for good. Keep us faithful in small things, and clean out whatever does not belong in Your house. Amen.
13.l: Pick a rhythm of rest or worship today that you tend to skip, and keep it.
q: Whose connections are you tempted to lean on that do not belong to your calling?
